title: Keep people informed, in their words
summary: Use the first two of Nielsen's usability heuristics to make any screen say what's happening, in words people know.
objective: Show people what's happening after every action, using everyday words instead of internal terms.

source.title: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design (Nielsen Norman Group)

hook.prompt: You tap **Save** in an app. It takes 4 seconds to finish, and nothing on screen changes meanwhile. What are many people likely to do?

options.feedback: Four seconds feels long when nothing moves. Without a sign of progress, people can't tell waiting from broken.

options.text: Tap Save again, thinking it didn't work
Assume it saved and close the app
options.feedback: Some will, and lose their work if it hadn't finished. But with no sign of progress, most people think their tap simply didn't register.

hook.explanation: With no sign that anything is happening, a working app looks exactly like a broken one. So people tap again, or give up.

bricks.title: Heuristic 1: show what's happening
bricks.body: Jakob Nielsen's **10 usability heuristics** are rules of thumb for spotting problems in an interface. The first is **visibility of system status**: after every action, show people what's going on, right away. Use a spinner for a short wait, a progress bar with time left for a long one, and a clear message like **Saved** when it's done.

term.definition: The interface always tells people what's going on, with feedback that comes right away.

visual.html:
Uploading photos

3 of 5 done · about 20 seconds left
visual.alt: A card titled Uploading photos, saying 3 of 5 done, about 20 seconds left, with a progress bar three-fifths full.

bricks.prompt: In a chat app, you tap **Send** and nothing changes for three seconds before the message appears. Which fix best follows the first heuristic?

options.text: Show the message at once, marked **Sending…**, then **Sent** when it arrives
Show a **Sent** label only once it's finished
options.feedback: That confirms the end, but the three silent seconds are still there. People need to see something the moment they tap.

options.text: Add a help page explaining that sending can take a few seconds
options.feedback: Nobody reads a help page mid-message. The status has to be on screen, at the moment it matters.
A bigger button is easier to tap, but it still doesn't tell anyone what's happening after they tap it.

bricks.hint: People need to know what's going on both right away and when it's done.
bricks.explanation: **Sending…** answers "did my tap work?" instantly, and **Sent** confirms the result. The status is visible from start to finish.

bricks.prompt: A large update takes several minutes to download. Which screen keeps people better informed?

visual.html: Downloading update
visual.alt: A Downloading update card with only a spinner and no other information.

options.feedback: A spinner says something is happening, but not how long it will take. For a wait of minutes, people need progress and time left.

visual.html:
Downloading update

40% · about 3 minutes left
visual.alt: A Downloading update card saying 40%, about 3 minutes left, with a progress bar two-fifths full.

bricks.hint: Is this a short wait or a long one?
bricks.explanation: For a long task, a progress bar with time left lets people decide whether to wait or do something else.

bricks.prompt: Which of these show people the system's status?

options.text: A badge showing **3** unread messages on the Inbox tab
**All changes saved** next to a document's title
The company logo at the top of every page
options.feedback: The logo stays the same whatever happens, so it tells people nothing about what's going on.

options.text: A **Contact us** link in the footer
options.feedback: Useful to have, but it's a way to get help, not a sign of what the system is doing or where you are.

bricks.hint: Which ones change as things happen?
bricks.explanation: Status isn't only loading. Unread counts, steps in a process, and save confirmations all tell people where things stand.

bricks.title: Heuristic 2: speak the user's language
bricks.body: The second heuristic is **match between the system and the real world**. Use words and ideas your users know from everyday life, not your team's internal terms or codes. **Error 0x80070005** means nothing to most people; **You don't have permission to open this file** does. Show information in the order people expect, too: the order they'd follow in real life.

term.word: Match between the system and the real world
term.definition: The interface uses words, ideas, and an order that are familiar to its users.

visual.html:
Error 0x80070005

Operation failed.

You can't open this file

You don't have permission. Ask its owner to share it with you.
visual.alt: Two messages: a red one saying Error 0x80070005, Operation failed; and a plain one saying You can't open this file, ask its owner to share it with you.

bricks.prompt: This is a shopping app's order screen. Tap the text that doesn't speak the customer's language.

visual.html:
Your order #4821

Status: FULFILLMENT_PENDING

Arrives Thursday

bricks.hint: Which line reads like it was written for the warehouse's computer, not for a shopper?
bricks.explanation: **FULFILLMENT_PENDING** is an internal code. A shopper would understand **Preparing your order**.

bricks.prompt: Match each internal term to the everyday words a user would understand.

pairs.right: Your card doesn't have enough funds

bricks.hint: Imagine saying each term out loud to a friend who has never built software.
bricks.explanation: Each everyday phrase says the same thing in words people already use, so nobody has to translate the screen.

bricks.prompt: A recipe app lists the steps in order, but sorts the ingredients alphabetically. In which order would a cook rather see the ingredients?

visual.html:
Pancakes: ingredients

  • Baking powder
  • Butter, melted
  • Eggs
  • Flour
  • Milk
  • Sugar
visual.alt: A pancake recipe card listing ingredients alphabetically: baking powder, butter, eggs, flour, milk, sugar.

options.text: In the order they're used in the steps
Alphabetically, as now, so each one is easy to find
options.feedback: Alphabetical order is tidy for a computer, but a cook works through the recipe step by step, not from A to Z.

options.text: From the largest amount to the smallest
options.feedback: That's logical on paper, but it doesn't match how cooking happens: you reach for things as each step needs them.

bricks.hint: Think about what the cook is doing while reading the list.
bricks.explanation: In the kitchen, you add ingredients as the steps call for them. Listing them in that order matches the real task.

challenge.prompt: Which fix would you ship first?
challenge.situation: In a food delivery app, people tap **Place order** and the screen stays the same for 5 seconds. Then it shows **Order status: QUEUED_FOR_DISPATCH**. Many people tap Place order twice and get two meals.

options.text: Show **Placing your order…** the moment they tap, then **Order confirmed: the restaurant is preparing your food**
options.outcome: People see their tap worked, stop ordering twice, and understand exactly where their food is.

options.text: Add a spinner during the 5 seconds, and keep the status text as it is
options.outcome: Double orders drop, but people are left puzzling over QUEUED_FOR_DISPATCH and some contact support to ask what it means.

options.text: Rename the status to **Waiting for a driver**, and keep the 5 silent seconds
options.outcome: The status now makes sense, but people still think their first tap failed and keep ordering twice.

options.text: Add an FAQ page that explains each status code
options.outcome: Hardly anyone opens it while ordering. The double orders and the confusing code both stay.

challenge.hint: There are two problems here: the silence, and the wording.
challenge.explanation: The screen breaks both heuristics: 5 silent seconds hide the status, and the code isn't the customer's language. The best fix solves both.

takeaways: After every action, show right away that something is happening, and confirm when it's done.
For long waits, show progress and time left, not just a spinner.
Write labels and messages in your users' everyday words, never internal codes.
Order information the way people use it in real life.
